column2: Salaries based on family “need budgets” and cut by 25% during the 1937-1938 year. Dreier writes to Aydelotte (April 1938) for advice and assistance, suggesting a job for Nell at the college, ideally an elementary school on the spot. Aydelotte replies (April 17) that Nell will take over the college library when the incumbent retires and that he will pay for her training at library school the following year. Aydelotte also pays for Nell's trips to Sullivan (Indiana) and supplements the college's finances and the medical expenses of Mary and Frank Rice. Rice never shows any resentment of this orchestrating role. A 25% salary cut for 1937-1938. Consequences: Nell prepared to become the college librarian.
Rice resumes a fairly steady round of lectures on education and the college, including several trips to Charleston and stops in Greensboro and Augusta.

Nell spends the fall between Sullivan and Swarthmore exploring library science programs, then returns to North Carolina for a library apprenticeship and courses at the Asheville Normal School in preparation for the UNC Chapel Hill program. She communicates cordially with her husband but does not want to try living together again. Mary begins her first year at Swarthmore; Frank, looking for work, stays a great deal at Aydelotte's home.

Robert Wunsch becomes the new rector. Some hope that Rice, a mere teacher again, will calm the animosities, but the Alberses and Dreier find it hard to recover their former relations with a Rice more sullen than repentant. The teachers more favorable to Rice (Sly, Bailey, Moellenhoff) are hardly vocal and do not sit on the Board of Fellows. Consequences: Rice's continued isolation.

Divorce from Nell (p. 180), the New York area, a second marriage, the Harper centenary prize (pp. 182, 186), moves to Florida, South Carolina, then Maryland, purchase of a farm (p. 195), a portrait painted by Chambers (p. 196), the Maryland commission on teacher training (pp. 200-201), death (pp. 9, 201).

Invited by Alfred Barr, director of the Museum of Modern Art, Bayer designs and installs the exhibition Bauhaus 1919–1928 (December 1938–January 1939), familiarizing the American public with the Bauhaus aesthetic exhibition “Bauhaus: 1919–1928,” December 1938 and January 1939 Consequences: Bayer becomes one of the first to bring the Bauhaus aesthetic into American life
The couple, who are Jewish, leave Czechoslovakia a year before the Reich moves in. Consequences: The house is despoiled and then damaged

At twenty, she leaves Brooklyn for Manhattan, drops out of Hunter College (mathematics) after a few weeks, and enrolls at the Leonardo da Vinci Art School and the American Artists School; Bob Jonas, director of the former, introduces her to Willem de Kooning. dual enrollment in two art schools popular with young artists Consequences: A decisive meeting with Bill, who will become her teacher and then her husband.

She leaves Paris, keeps a studio in San Francisco for three years, then five years at Soda Springs in the High Sierra, with many trips into the Nevada desert. 3 years in San Francisco, 5 years at Soda Springs Consequences: the desert leaves a lasting mark on her work

After Christmas, Rice shuts himself up in his study, sulking and sucking on his pipe, while the community is divided between revulsion and sympathy. The infatuation cools when it becomes clear that the girl prefers another student, but the indignation remains and reopens all the old grievances. Consequences: Rice's support among his colleagues is exhausted

Jonas brings Elaine into the immaculate studio; a battleship-gray floor, a canvas of a bald man in ocher and olive green on the easel; she has never seen anything like it; that very evening she confesses to her sister Words: Elaine to Marjorie about falling in love; Marjorie: it was pretty instantaneous, although she was very involved with Milton Atmosphere: Mystery and certainty; the order of the place against the emotion Stakes: The meeting that changes Elaine's life

Bill composes the still life (coffeepot, shell, yellow cup, blue shirt, army blanket); for three months she paints while he talks about the spaces between the objects; she sometimes goes to lie down, brain-tired Words: Listening to de Kooning talk about two inches made her brain-tired; as if one had never seen a cup Atmosphere: Seduction through teaching; exhausting concentration Stakes: Elaine becomes a docile student and a lover

The morning after Dick Porter's death, a general meeting; Moellenhoff speaks of the group's guilt in the face of the boy's loneliness, and of chosen loneliness Words: loneliness is very often chosen and self-imposed Atmosphere: shock, guilt, clinical dignity Stakes: how a community answers for a death it did not see coming

A total spectacle in the round: an original score by Evarts, the orchestra under Sly, a masked and caped audience forming the outer circles. Atmosphere: An immersive ceremony, a multimedia celebration. Stakes: A forgotten anticipation of the 1952 Cage event.

A young man from the Bronx, torn between the New Bauhaus and Black Mountain, dines with the former Bauhaus student who has come to recruit him; Schawinsky's charm tips the balance. Atmosphere: A restaurant on the Hudson, a charming conversation. Stakes: The choice of a life.

Rice, withdrawn into several rooms of Lee Hall, discreetly invites his supporters; he gives a room number and enjoins silence. Words: he will be in such-and-such a room, but tell no one. Atmosphere: hushed clandestinity Stakes: The founder reduced to an underground existence in his own college

After an ardent pursuit, Bill offers to teach Elaine and invites her to paint in his own studio; she is overjoyed; they become lovers, as everyone could have predicted. Atmosphere: The master's magnetism; celebrated by their circle. Stakes: The birth of the central couple of the New York School.

As they walk, Rice explains that he knows Alice a little better than the other students because she needs to be brought out, to feel important; with a little attention, she will blossom. Words: Rice: she “needed to be brought out,” “to feel important,” she “blossom[ed]” with a little attention. Atmosphere: Confidential, paternal — the image of a good father watching over his flock, which barely masks desire. Stakes: The gap between the mentor's talk and the budding affair.

Rice borrows a small beach cottage and works on his writing about his Southern youth. In the spring he visits Louis and Stella Adamic in Milford (New Jersey), who push and encourage him. Nell leaves for a long stay at Swarthmore. Rice expects to return by May 1 at the latest, rested. A small beach cottage; meals of crabs, oysters, and beer with visitors.

Rice is given leave until May 1; he may return only if he and the faculty agree; around mid-April he is to obtain the faculty's informal opinion through the secretary, Mangold. The community also decides that Alice should not be penalized for what was not mainly her doing, which absolves her of responsibility and makes Rice a Svengali. Consequences: Rice's departure; the start of the power struggle.

In mid-April, Rice writes the agreed letter asking the faculty's disposition; ten days later, the Board of Fellows votes unanimously to extend his leave until September and credits his bank account with 100 dollars for living expenses. Mangold argues in particular that Nell, still hurt, with the divorce unresolved, cannot live in the community with him. 100 dollars paid into his bank account, pending the final adjustment of the total allowance. Consequences: Rice takes the news badly.

When four members of the faculty come to tell him of the decision, Rice tells them angrily that people are thinking only of the good of the college and not of his, and that it is indecent to have decided without seeing him and gauging his state of mind.

At the last community meeting of the year, Wunsch explains that Rice has shown poor judgment and dissipated his leadership; the faculty has in effect told him to go and see whether the college can live without him, while hoping to find him again in the fall as he was at the beginning. Consequences: Reconciliation left open.
Meetings of the Board of Fellows (June 2, 1938) and the General Meeting of May 1938; Mangold writes to Rice on May 27. Consequences: Rice leaves the college

Four members of the faculty come to tell Rice that his leave has been extended; he answers angrily that they have thought only of the good of the college and not of his own, and that it was indecent to decide without seeing him or gauging his state of mind. Words: “People were thinking only of what was good for the College and not of what was good” for him. Atmosphere: A bitter confrontation by the sea. Stakes: Rice's trust in the community broken for good.

At the last community meeting of the year, Wunsch sums up: Rice has shown poor judgment and dissipated his leadership; the faculty has told him to go and see whether the college can live without him; many have missed his conversation and his practical wisdom and hope to find him again in the fall as he was at the beginning. Words: “You have often said that the place should not be a one-man college; give us a chance to prove that it isn't”. Atmosphere: Sobriety, qualified hope. Stakes: The community takes back its own founding myth.

To reaffirm its confidence, the Board votes an additional 200 dollars for living expenses and asks Rice to represent the college at a meeting of progressive schools in Chicago; he refuses. An additional 200 dollars. Consequences: A sign of Rice's ambivalence.

Rice returns in the fall but now leads a ghostly existence, a deposed monarch. No one wants the post of rector; Rice believes it was Mrs. Albers who coveted it for her husband; the Board finally votes it to Wunsch. Rice judges Wunsch a nice, sweet fellow but incapable of leading; he thinks Mangold and Albers are using Wunsch to govern in his place. Rice spends his time in an upstairs room of Lee Hall writing his autobiography, begun at Folly Beach. Consequences: Rice gives up teaching and community affairs.

Back again, Rice barely takes part in college life. He settles into several rooms of Lee Hall and spends his time writing and talking with his most ardent students. If he wants to see someone, he says he is in such-and-such a room, but tell no one. Only the students in the writing seminar see him regularly. Secret appointments by room number.

His ironic and literary two-part reminiscence of his mother's family is published in Harper's Magazine in November and December 1938 — the first installments of an episodic autobiography about his youth and the post-Civil War South. Published in two parts.

Shortly after his arrival in the United States, Herbert Bayer visits the major exhibition Bauhaus: 1919–1928 at MoMA, which introduces the American public to the achievements of the Bauhaus in every field of design, a school that the German regime — soon to be America's official enemy — had brutally closed. Exhibition from December 1938 to January 1939 Consequences: The American public discovers the achievements of the Bauhaus

Shortly after his arrival in the United States, Bayer attends the major exhibition Bauhaus: 1919-1928, which reveals to the American public the school's successes in every field of design, a school brutally closed by the regime that is about to become America's official enemy. Exhibition from December 1938 to January 1939. Consequences: The American public discovers the Bauhaus.

A socially progressive school calling for a new, aggressive, and independent art, without slavish imitation of the teacher; she works there as a model so as not to pay the fees Sculpture with Milton Hebald, watercolor with Ben Wilson, oil painting with Nahum Tschacbasov; an introduction to lithography, etching, and silkscreen; Wednesday evening lectures; Goya, Daumier, and the Mexican muralists as models Consequences: The birth of her lifelong sympathy for people she believes unjustly treated, including convicted criminals

At twenty-one, of age, she escapes parental authority and moves in with him; she nonetheless continues to see Resnick Her mother required her to be home by 10 p.m. as long as she was a minor Consequences: The start of a romantic pattern (other men) that will last for decades

Albers, who had not made a lithograph since about 1917 in Germany, discovers the lithographer Dosamantes and creates a series of four large lithographs with organic forms and velvety lines. Four large-format lithographs

At the end of the summer of 1939, Meza, a protégé of the critic Helm, spends a week in Oaxaca with the Alberses; before a monumental torso by Meza, Albers declares “Me convence,” high praise for a twenty-year-old artist. Meza then paints a carpeta of thirty-two watercolors Consequences: A deep impression on the young Meza

Josef Albers makes lithographs at the Taller de Gráfica Popular in 1939; he will later reuse the back of one of them as the support for an oil study. A study on the back of a torn Mexican lithograph, an emerald-green line on a brown ground, bordered with dark purple and ultramarine

Michael van Beuren, a former student of Albers's at the Bauhaus, settles in Mexico in 1939; with Klaus Grabe (another Bauhäusler) and Morley Webb, his firm Domus manufactures Porset's butacas. Hannes Meyer also arrives in 1939; Max Cetto and then Mathias Goeritz, linked for a time with Barragán, complete this circle of German émigrés.
Van Beuren accompanies the Alberses to the monastery: Josef is interested in the colonial architecture and in the way people live; Anni in the weavings and local art.

At the end of the summer of 1939, the young Mexican Guillermo Meza (20) spends a week with Helm in the company of the Alberses and Alex Reed; he draws from it a folio of 32 gouaches, highly varied in design and color. Before one of Meza's monumentally conceived torsos, Albers declares: “I am convinced by that”. 32 gouaches; Meza is 20 Consequences: Albers, a born teacher, makes a strong impression on the young artist.

Albers, who had not practiced lithography since about 1917 in Germany, discovers the lithographer Francisco Dosamantes at the TGP (a collective founded in 1938, devoted to art for social change) and creates a suite of four large lithographs titled Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta. rich, velvety lines, swirling forms, organic swellings evoking life and growth Consequences: Belies the image of Albers as a strict geometer and cold rationalist.

Albers makes lithographs; an oil study on paper painted on the back of one of them shows a linear structure in bright emerald green, perhaps drawn with a drawing pen, a line modulated in tone and width on a brown ground. Emerald green, a brown rectangle, a drawing pen

Albers makes lithographs at the Taller de Gráfica Popular in 1939; an oil study on paper [Cat. 110] is painted on the back of one of them: a luminous emerald-green line, probably done with a pen, on a brown rectangle, framed by deep purple and then dark ultramarine. A line modulated in tone and thickness, evoking floors and walls, doors and windows, inside and outside at once. Consequences: Illustrates the move from the controlled line of 1936 toward pictorial experiment.

American citizenship. Three months in Mexico (June 8 – September 8, based at Calle de Paris 23); Josef teaches at Gobert College in Tlalpan in August (lodging at Allende 2); the lithographs Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta printed at the Taller de Gráfica Popular. The Fleischmanns flee Nazi Germany and arrive in Veracruz on June 22 on the Orinoco, met by Josef and Anni; Toni's diary swings between joy and the despair of emigrants. the same ship, the Orinoco, as in 1937

Having entered the United States in 1939, informed by the National Coordinating Committee to Aid Refugees of a vacancy at Black Mountain, he is hired quickly and settles there with his wife and daughter for the 1939-1940 academic year Consequences: Becomes the most beloved figure at the college

In a speech, Albers states his motto: teachers have no right to demand of their students what they are unable or unwilling to do themselves. The exact wording: “We as teachers have no right to demand from our students what we are unable or unwilling to do ourselves”. Consequences: This statement sums up his system of beliefs and links passionate painting with devoted teaching.

During a trip to Mexico in the summer of 1939, Albers interviews several candidates for a teaching post at Black Mountain and reports his reactions in letters to his colleague Fred D. Mangold. He wants someone who will not duplicate his own teaching and who will model independence. Remarks in his letters: one candidate so inflexible and empty; another without enough independence; another he feared was a communist. Consequences: A disappointing search; no hiring from this trip is mentioned.
From 1939 on, Albers regularly gives summer courses and other short sessions at Harvard.

Driven from his post in Cologne in 1933 by a Nazi purge, after six more years in Europe, Jalowetz takes up the open post at Black Mountain with his wife Johanna, who teaches bookbinding and singing there. the conductor's post in Cologne lost in 1933; 6 years in Europe before emigrating Consequences: Jalowetz becomes the college's music teacher

The college commissions from Gropius and Breuer a complex of academic buildings for the Lake Eden campus, which would have been their first major project in the United States; the chronic lack of money prevents construction. Consequences: The project is never carried out; the model shown at MoMA.

Walter Gropius and Marcel Breuer unveil a plan for the Studies Building in a modernist style inspired by the Bauhaus. construction estimated at 50,000 dollars, beyond the college's means Consequences: In 1940, Kocher is hired to adjust these dreams to reality; his own plan is finally adopted.

From the late 1930s, on many trips to Mexico and Latin America, the Alberses — especially Anni — take an interest in ideograms and hieroglyphs, bringing these interests into their art and teaching and inspiring Ruth Asawa and Ray Johnson. Consequences: precedes Olson's interest in glyphs

In his text “Art—A Constant,” Albers distinguishes the medium serving an outside end from the medium for its own sake, like the words of reporting versus the words of poetry. Text reprinted in On Designing (Wesleyan University Press, 1971, p. 46)

An anthology of short stories coedited by Wunsch and Edna Albers for the PEA's Commission on Human Relations, with writing exercises, meant to stimulate classroom discussion. Moral stories on optimism, modesty, kindness, loyalty; exercises in “written biographies” and dramatic sketches on the characters' earlier lives Consequences: Illustrates the moral role assigned to literature in Wunsch's teaching

Wunsch and Edna Albers coedit Thicker Than Water: Stories of Family Life (D. Appleton-Century), with a foreword by Alice V. Keliher. Edna Albers was not related to Josef and Anni Albers. Publisher: D. Appleton-Century Company.

Walter Gropius and Marcel Breuer are commissioned to design the college's new buildings on the Lake Eden property; the project, resolutely modern, is later abandoned for lack of funds. Buildings linked by covered walkways, irregular angles following the shore, a study building on stilts over the lake, a meeting room with a panoramic curved glass wall, a roof terrace with a parabolic windbreak wall Consequences: Plans abandoned for lack of money, but a sign of the college's openness to modern design
Josef makes out the figure 3 in an aerial view of the road “The Loop”; with stenciled blue paint he accentuates the 3 and adds a 9 for a 1939 New Year's card. stenciled blue paint
Albers tells his students that Black Mountain is consciously on the side of the Maya Indians, the ancient Americans being THE representatives of abstract art.

One Thursday afternoon in 1939, the father writes a birthday letter to his son Fee (who will be ten the following summer): he asks whether it is still snowing in Kirkwood and whether he can go sledding; he describes the deep pit between the buildings of Rockefeller Center, flooded and frozen in winter for skating, skaters in colorful costumes, professionals among them; he himself goes back indoors to the warmth, turning up his collar, keeping his nose warm. A pit a block long; a frozen rink; Fee soon to be 10 Consequences: Fee is very probably the young Fielding Dawson (a hypothesis) — material for a flashback on the childhood separated from the father.

A 1939 letter reproduced: “Aunty Dot bought me a teddy bear and I named it butterscotch!”; finger paintings at school (“tornado over the Picific”), Miss Trilift the art teacher and her “jungle scene”. A teddy bear named Butterscotch; a finger painting, “tornado over the Picific”
Albers declares in a lecture that the indirect influence of the teacher's being and doing is more effective and contagious than is believed: one can develop others only by developing oneself.
A lecture given by Albers on truthfulness in art, a typescript cited in the notes

At the end of the 1938-1939 year, Rice negotiates with publishers over his book and with the faculty over a leave for the fall semester of 1939. The faculty asks him to take a whole year, 1939-1940, instead; to keep up an appearance of controlling his own fate, he refuses and repeats his request for a single semester, granted reluctantly — leaving some teachers angry at having given in.

With the pipes of her country house south of Denver frozen, Elizabeth Paepcke finds refuge for her skiing guests in Aspen, a nearly abandoned former mining town frozen pipes, the need for a place to ski Consequences: she brings her husband there in 1945

Anni must get her extended family out of Nazi Germany; her parents' ship docks at Veracruz, where she and Josef have to bribe one person after another before her increasingly desperate mother and her father can finally disembark; Anni attributes her chronic anxiety directly to this period. Consequences: Anni Albers's lasting chronic anxiety

They become American citizens without celebrating as they had with the Kandinskys eleven years earlier in Dessau, when the latter became German citizens, but overwhelmed with joy. On her passport, Anni gives her occupation as “housewife”: “artist” seems pretentious to her (a word she will never use for herself), “weaver” reductive; the author sees in this the expression of the Bauhaus wish to give value to everyday domestic life. occupation entered: “housewife”

Both become American citizens; they do not celebrate as they had with the Kandinskys eleven years earlier in Dessau, when the latter had become German citizens, but are overwhelmed with joy. Consequences: A permanent anchoring in the United States.

A first trade with Milton Resnick; the collection will reach more than a thousand works over fifty years, made up of birthday gifts and purchases to help friends or young artists (moral encouragement or money, usually both). more than a thousand works over fifty years
Elaine meets Gorky around 1939 through Bill; she will tell Rose Slivka in 1982 that she was already deeply committed to being an artist.

At twenty-nine, Kline exhibits in a stall at the Washington Square Show, flanked by Otto Botto and Earl Kerkam; the manufacturer David Orr buys a small painting of the Ninth Avenue El, the first of more than a hundred and fifty works he will acquire in twelve years. Kline is 29; Orr will end up owning more than 150 works in 12 years; a Lehigh Valley scene painted from memory without sketches wins a prize at the National Academy in 1944 Consequences: Orr's lasting patronage: portraits of his Long Island family, still lifes, landscapes, commissions from verbal descriptions (a synagogue from a vague photograph, a brown and luminous result in the manner of Rembrandt)

Orr becomes his most active patron: he buys about a hundred and fifty paintings during the forties, commissions many portraits of himself and his family, and constantly suggests subjects and scenes. about 150 paintings bought during the 1940s Consequences: funds Kline's survival; he had a studio set up at Orr's

Thursday afternoon: after writing to his daughter, the father writes to his son, who will be ten the following summer; a description of the frozen pit between the buildings, skaters in colorful costumes, professionals; he turns up his collar and goes back into the warmth. Words: he likes to keep his toes and his little nose nice and warm. Atmosphere: Fatherly tenderness made a little awkward by distance. Stakes: The absent father trying to exist through detail and humor.
Two years after 4 Painters, the Addison shows Albers's recent paintings, including Four X's (1939), In the Soil (1938), Related Reds (1938). Consequences: The Albers–Addison bond consolidated

In April 1939 the Addison presents MoMA's exhibition Bauhaus 1919-1928; shortly afterward, Sawyer leaves to direct the Worcester Art Museum; Bartlett Hayes succeeds him. Consequences: Hayes will direct Albers's later exhibitions at the Addison (1940, late 1911)

Rice's cousin publishes a long letter to the editor pointing out factual errors in “Grandmother Smith's Plantation” and defending Senator Smith against the insinuation that he defended the right to lynch. The errors pointed out concern mainly the physical layout of the plantation and incidents placed in the wrong spot. Consequences: Rice replies by citing the Congressional Record of April 16, 1935; the threatened libel suit never materializes.

In his reply, Rice asserts that he made no deliberate factual error and cites Senator Smith's speech of April 16, 1935, against an antilynching bill, in which the senator defended going outside the law to protect the virtue of our women and called the law this infamous law. Smith spoke of the just punishment to be meted out to the beast who invades that sanctuary. Consequences: The uncle's racist positions are publicly exposed.

They see Guernica in May at the Valentine Gallery, then the Picasso retrospective opens at MoMA in November; the immense canvas transmutes current events (the German bombing of Guernica) into anguished testimony Consequences: The bull, Picasso's alter ego, foreshadows Elaine's future fascination with this animal

A governess at home from the age of 5, weekly correspondence courses. At 8, a new teacher assigned her to write a story about anything she liked; the child wrote the story of a little girl who disobeys, goes to the lake to see a green-eyed frog, and drowns. The father, on his daily visit to the schoolroom, called it “pathetic dribble,” tore the sheet from the little desk, and ripped it up. He died fourteen months later in the French Resistance. tutoring from the age of 5; weekly visit to the correspondence school; May 1939; father killed in the Resistance in 1940 Consequences: Gray connects this scene with the symbolic parricide experienced with Olson

At eight, the child is given a free subject for the first time and writes a miniature of minimalist severity: a girl disobeys, goes to the lake to see a green-eyed frog who holds the key to freedom, and immediately drowns. the full text of the story; an evening in May 1939 Consequences: The father tears up the sheet

On his daily visit to the schoolroom, the father thunders (“Pathetic dribble!”), tears the sheet from the little desk, and rips it to pieces, predicting what will become of her if she never finishes anything. He dies fourteen months later in the French Resistance. “Pathetic dribble!”; the sheet torn up; May 1939, the father's death in 1940 Consequences: The first male “censor” in a series; the ban on writing

A new teacher orders her to write a story about anything she likes. The child, between excitement and terror, writes the minimal fable of a little girl who disobeys, goes to see a green-eyed frog who holds the key to freedom, and promptly drowns. The father, on his daily visit, storms (“You dare call that a story?”), tears the sheet from the little desk, and rips it up. He dies fourteen months later in the Resistance. Words: Father: “Pathetic dribble! ... What will become of you if you never finish anything!” Atmosphere: the terror and excitement of a new freedom, then paternal fury Stakes: A first failed parricide, replayed and accomplished with Olson at Black Mountain

The father's daily visit to the schoolroom: he takes the sheet, reads it, thunders, and tears the paper to pieces over the little desk Words: “Pathetic dribble! You dare call that a story? What will become of you if you never finish anything!” Atmosphere: a May evening; the child's excitement and terror at the freedom of the subject Stakes: the first censor, the ban on writing, the matrix of all the future work

Shortly after arriving, Anni writes to a friend at Black Mountain (Anne Mangold, letter of June 15, 1939): a first party with painters and Americans, ending at 1:30 a.m. in a bachelor's apartment with a supper at 11 p.m. Letter of June 15, 1939

Albers makes a montage of 62 contact prints titled “Tenayuca, juin 1939,” supplemented by another montage combining a press photograph and 30 contact prints. 62 contact prints on cardboard, 25.7 x 40.6 cm

Shortly after their arrival, Anni writes to a friend at Black Mountain: a first evening with painters and Americans, a little crazy, which went on until 1:30, ending at a bachelor's place with a supper at 11 p.m.; exhausted the next day. a party until 1:30, supper at 11 p.m.

Rice leaves the college at the end of June 1939. Nell remains firm in her intentions and does not want to be near him. Rice says he wants to find lodgings near Adamic. A faculty member writes that it is clear no one is in a hurry to have him around. a letter from one teacher to another, late June 1939 Consequences: The idea of preventing his return for good gains ground; by the end of 1939, the prevailing opinion is that his formal resignation must be requested.

Rice hoped to follow Nell to Chapel Hill to write and attempt a reconciliation; she rejects the plan. When he leaves Black Mountain in June, it is for Southern Pines. Nell stays at Black Mountain, finishing her work at the Asheville Normal School before leaving for Chapel Hill. Frank and Mary come back for the summer and take jobs at the nearby Lake Eden Inn. Summer jobs at the Lake Eden Inn.

A party with painters and Americans, a little crazy, that goes on until 1:30 a.m., ending in a bachelor's apartment with a supper at 11 p.m.; exhaustion the next day Words: Anni's letter to Anne Mangold: the party was “todo un poco loco” Atmosphere: Nocturnal, exuberant
Josef teaches in August at Gobert College in Tlalpan. Trips to Morelia, Pátzcuaro, Guadalajara. A series of lithographs, Alfa, Beta, Gamma, Delta, printed at the Taller de Gráfica Popular.
Four letters from Albers to Mangold dated June 29, July 8, and August 7, 1939, preserved in the JAAF archives. Exact dates: 1939-06-29, 1939-07-08, 1939-08-07.

A long correspondence about the college's obligation to pay a $145 bill that Rice incurred in a car accident; probably a triggering factor in the final break. $145; Steinau's letters, Sept. 1939–Feb. 1940; Dreier to Steinau (Oct. 4, 1939) speaks of behavior bordering on dishonesty Consequences: A precipitating factor in Rice's final departure

Urged on by his friends Louis and Stella Adamic, whom Rice visits regularly in Milford (New Jersey), Rice proposes an autobiography to Adamic's publisher; after two sample chapters, the senior editor, Cass Canfield, accepts at once. Canfield: it is certainly rare to receive a manuscript with so much charm (letter of October 20, 1939). Consequences: A contract with a 500-dollar advance.

Harper advises cutting several chapters of personal opinion and working the views into the narrative: a chapter on progressive education (the latest fashion of bandwagons), on normal schools, on the people of the Middle West, and a chapter titled “The Gentleman, the Lady, and the Negro: Three Teachers of the South and Three Fictions”. The ideas are eventually folded into the chapters on Webb School, Tulane, Oxford, the University of Nebraska, and Rollins.

Anni Albers writes a theoretical text concluding that the work of art is both reality and vision, that nature is inexhaustible, and that art is constant and complete in itself. essay dated “November, 1939”

Dissatisfied with his working title, “From South Carolina to the Present,” Rice repeats in a letter to Canfield the sentence from a speech in Cambridge (Massachusetts) about having come out of the eighteenth century; Canfield underlines the sentence and proposes I Came Out of the Eighteenth Century. Rice had said in Cambridge that he was born in the eighteenth century in South Carolina; his working title was “From South Carolina to the Present”. Consequences: The final title is found.

The Picasso retrospective, from the Demoiselles d'Avignon to Guernica (a 25.5-foot painting accompanied by some sixty studies), proves “staggering” for de Kooning; Elaine judges it enormously important. Preceded in May by a showing of Guernica at the Valentine Gallery organized by the American Artists' Congress. Guernica: 25.5 feet wide, about 60 studies; three Weeping Women included; the Demoiselles d'Avignon entered MoMA in 1939 through the Lillie P. Bliss bequest Consequences: An immediate response: Two Standing Men in pencil, transmuting Guernica's aggression into frozen immobility; the restrained ferocity will later burst out in the women

Over about two months from Christmas 1939, Wunsch pays Rice several visits in his Southern Pines retreat to obtain his resignation. First visit: a game of cat and mouse; Rice determined not to let him make the request; Wunsch overstays his time and then leaves without speaking frankly. He then writes to Rice that he fully enjoyed the visit and found a man who was calm, friendly, and wise, with something of the old spirit. Consequences: The first attempt fails.
A lecture on education and art teaching, given in December 1939; a typewritten manuscript; quotation taken from page 2

Seated by chance next to the Dutch painter Sanders, Elaine, intrigued by their shared nationality, introduces him to de Kooning Consequences: A first example of her lifelong inclination to bring together people with common interests

The middle-aged composer invites her into his studio-library of electronic sounds; he plays her a manipulated kissing sound that reminds her of a lion's roar He takes her on a “tour” — five Italian ice-cream parlors to taste the best flavors
